q: Madeira is either heated artificially over a matter of months or left to ripen in cask in a hot loft over many years. What is the slow, unforced route called?
exp: Canteiro is the name of the wooden rack the cask rests on, up under the roof where the sun does the work. Artificial heat comes either from a warmed tank, held at forty-five to fifty degrees for at least three months, or from an armazem de calor, a cask store warmed more gently for six months or more, and both serve the commercial blends.

q: Someone opening a meal wants the leanest, most bracing thing on the Madeira list. Which of these varieties goes in the glass?
exp: The classic ladder runs Sercial, Verdelho, Bual, then Malvasia, and Malvasia is the one sold as Malmsey. Terrantez is a rare noble variety that sits outside that four. Sercial is planted highest and coolest on the island and finishes almost dry, which is why it works before the food rather than after it.

q: Sweetness in a fortified wine is settled at a single moment during the ferment. When is a Malmsey fortified relative to a Sercial?
opts: Only after the wine has already been heated
Later, once the yeast has worked through almost all the sugar
Earlier, while a great deal of sugar is still unfermented
At exactly the same point, with sugar added afterwards
exp: Spirit kills the yeast, so whatever sugar remains at that moment stays in the wine for good. Fortifying early leaves a sweet wine and fortifying late a dry one, which is the whole mechanism behind the four styles.

q: A single-year Madeira labelled Frasqueira has spent how long in cask before it may be bottled?
exp: Frasqueira, or vintage Madeira, is the top of the hierarchy and comes from one variety and one harvest. Colheita is the shorter single-vintage category, released after five years.

q: Blends labelled simply Reserve or Rainwater are generally built on one workhorse variety rather than on the classic whites. Which grape?
exp: Tinta Negra is hardy, adaptable and can be vinified at any sweetness level, which makes it the backbone of the commercial range. Sercial, Verdelho, Bual and Malvasia are reserved for the more expensive bottlings.

q: Vines on Pico grow inside thousands of small enclosures walled in black volcanic stone, a landscape on the UNESCO list. What are the enclosures called?
exp: Each curral is a few square metres of lava cleared to bare rock and walled to break the Atlantic wind and hold the day's heat into the night. The wines that come off them are unmistakably saline.

q: Two Azorean DOCs, Pico and Biscoitos, built their historic export reputation on a single white variety also grown on Madeira. Which?
exp: Verdelho crossed from Madeira to the islands and gave a strong, partly oxidative white that travelled well by sea. Both islands still make a fortified licoroso from it, but the modern revival has been driven by crisp, saline dry whites.

q: Tiny berries, thick skins, a stingy crop and a scent of violets and bergamot describe Portugal's most admired black grape. Which?
exp: Low yields nearly saw it abandoned before selection work in the Dao and the Douro rescued it. Colour, tannin and perfume all arrive in unusual concentration, which is why a little of it goes a long way in a blend.

q: An early-ripening, low-acid white with a loud floral and citrus perfume answers to Maria Gomes in Bairrada. What is it called elsewhere?
exp: One grape with two names in neighbouring regions, which is entirely normal in Portugal. Its aromatics arrive early and fade fast, so it is picked promptly and drunk young.

q: Asked for the Portuguese white grape that Spain calls Albarino, a sommelier should say what?
exp: One grape, one river, two countries: Rias Baixas grows it in Galicia and Moncao e Melgaco grows it across the Minho. In both places it gives fuller, more stone-fruited wine than the varieties around it.

q: Old vineyards in the Douro and in Portalegre were planted with dozens of varieties intermingled and are still picked all together. What is that arrangement called?
exp: Nobody recorded what was planted where, so the blending happens in the vineyard rather than the cellar. Vinha velha on a Portuguese label usually points to exactly this, and the spread of ripening dates is part of why the wines balance.

q: Spicy, herbal and badly prone to rot in a wet autumn, one Alentejo black grape is known in the north as Tinta Amarela. What is its southern name?
exp: Trincadeira lends lift and spice to blends dominated by Aragonez and Alicante Bouschet, but thin skins and tight bunches make it a liability in a damp year. Dry Alentejo heat is precisely what it needs.

q: Bark is stripped from a cork oak in summer and the tree is then left alone for a fixed period before the next harvest. How long?
exp: Portuguese law sets the minimum at nine years, and the tree regrows its bark without being felled or otherwise damaged. A cork oak is usually not stripped at all until it is about twenty-five years old.

q: The first two strippings of a cork oak never become wine stoppers. Why not?
opts: The bark is toxic to wine at that age
The tree is legally protected until its third stripping
The first two harvests are reserved for the state
The bark is too coarse and irregular for a stopper
exp: Virgin and secondary cork go to flooring, insulation and shoe soles. Only from the third harvest, more than forty years into the tree's life, does the bark have the uniform cell structure a stopper needs.

q: Drawing a stopper at the table, a sommelier finds a body of glued cork granules finished with a disc of solid cork at each end. What sort of closure is that?
opts: A colmated cork, one solid piece whose surface pits have been filled with cork dust
A technical cork, an agglomerated body capped with natural cork discs
A synthetic stopper extruded from food-grade polymer
A natural cork, punched in one piece from a single strip of bark
exp: The granules are the offcuts left after whole corks are punched from the bark, and the discs put natural cork where the wine actually touches. Stoppers built this way cost a fraction of a one-piece cork and are meant for wine drunk within a few years, since the glue line is not built for decades. A colmated cork is a different economy again: one solid piece whose lenticels have been packed with cork dust to smooth it.

q: A red labelled Garrafeira has met an ageing requirement that plain Reserva does not. What is it?
opts: At least twelve months in new oak barrels
At least thirty months in total, twelve of them in bottle
At least five years in the producer's own cellar
At least twenty-four months in cask, with no bottle minimum
exp: Reserva asks only for a stated vintage and alcohol half a degree above the regional minimum. Garrafeira adds the time, and the compulsory spell in glass is what gives those wines their settled, secondary character.
